biography.plain_text: Robert Stewart of Ingliston was a Scottish distiller and landowner who owned the large Kirkliston distillery near Edinburgh. He expanded his business by acquiring a second distillery at Queensferry. His wider commercial interests included chairing Caledonian Insurance and the New Zealand and Australian Land Company, where he was an original shareholder.

long_biography.plain_text:
At Kinlochmoidart, Robert Stewart commissioned William Leiper to build a new house in 1884. The Scottish Baronial design combined grey stone with red sandstone dressings brought from Ayrshire and a green slate roof. Inside, it incorporated plate glass, plumbing and hydroelectric power.

The new mansion stood beside its predecessor, which Stewart retained as stables and service accommodation. Leiper's work for him extended to entrance lodges, a cottage at Brunary and a school at Kinacara. The house hosted sporting-season gatherings, and the estate passed to Stewart's son John after his death in 1909.

Input Kalizma dates begin in 1904, while independent accounts give construction in 1906. Design and commissioning can predate launch; no input relationship is changed. The exact personal identity is reinforced by Ingliston-Kinlochmoidart links in contemporary records.

The later General Robert Stewart is his grandson, and John is his son. A Kirkliston gravestone for a Robert Stewart who died in 1904 is not this owner. The Baltimore distiller with the same name and medieval Stewart nobles are also excluded.

The principal original-wealth inference is qualitative: ownership of a large distillery, active acquisition of another, independent identification as a distilling businessman and explicit retrospective wealth attribution. No company total or estate acreage is equated to personal net worth.

Terminal Food & Beverage is an explicit origin fallback. The retained country estate and earlier corporate shareholding are positive assets, but their balance against other holdings cannot be established. A country house does not alone prove a real-estate investment or agricultural operating fortune.

The origin mechanism is Unknown. Acquisitions show expansion but do not settle earlier capital formation. The Parks Canada account identifies John Stewart and his son J. C. separately; it does not establish that Robert inherited from either. No family-transfer route is invented.

Investor is the strongest relationship alternative, based on purchased assets and original company shareholding. The evidence does not establish a personally material active investment mandate at death. Historical chairmanship alone cannot supply that premise; Unknown remains the terminal decision.

The death day is resolved from a contemporary newspaper's Tuesday reference in its Saturday 30 January 1909 issue. The year is independently corroborated. Birth year follows an exact official authority record; no birth day, month or birthplace is proposed.

Official heritage records date the estate purchase to 1882, while the clan history gives May 1883. House chronology also varies between commission and completion dates. The biography uses the explicit 1884 commission and avoids the disputed purchase year.

Forbes was checked first. Searches covered all supported personal link types: LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook, Twitter/X, Youtube, TikTok, Personal Website, Vimeo, Flickr, Trip Advisor and Zillow, plus Wikipedia and Company Website. Modern namesakes, third-party house photographs and descendant estate pages are not his personal accounts.

No personal Wikipedia page or Forbes profile was verified. The vessel's Wikipedia page is not a person link. The historic owner's absence from modern platforms is consistent with his death date, but no matching commemorative endpoint was verified either.

Spirits & distilling is the sole minimal active tag. Insurance chairmanship is documented but omitted as a tag because a personally defining long-term operating mandate is less clear. No tag is invented for an unrepresented fact.

The long biography covers his commissioned building and concrete design decisions, not descendant restoration or private yacht ownership. Its technical features describe the historic building rather than claiming he invented or personally designed them.

PDFs for the firsthand memoir and contemporary death notice were directly downloaded into memory and extracted. Indexed source bodies and the limited yacht preview are identified individually. No inaccessible source is represented as fully read.
